Therefore, it is based on a literature review and class discussions of a wide range of topics in biology, chemistry, mathematics, physics, and geology, related to the biological processes and biological systems. In addition to bibliography-based presentations and discussions, the students also have the opportunity to present their ongoing research projects and link them to the different topics covered in the literature review part.
courses.prerequisiteText: COSS711 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: COSS711 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Journal Club
courses.description: Graduate students will participate in all departmental seminars and journal clubs and attend seminars presented by guest speakers. Each graduate student should present and discuss data obtained from their dissertation research or present one seminar per semester in advanced topics of contemporary Science. The student should gain practice reading primary scientific literature, writing scientific blogs, and asking analytical questions.

courses.title: Astronomy
courses.description: This general education course aims at developing a clear understanding of the basics of astronomy. It deals with: Getting to Know the sky, Figuring out how things work, The Family of the sun, The Sun, our very own Star, Learning about Stars, Understanding Stars, Galaxies and Cosmology.

courses.title: Conceptual Physics
courses.description: This general education course aims at developing a clear understanding of the physical concepts which play an important role in our daily life. It deals with the following subjects: Mechanics and Laws of Motion, Properties of Matter, Heat, Electricity and Magnetism, Waves and Vibrations, Sound and Light.

courses.title: General Physics I
courses.description: This course aims at developing a clear understanding of the basic concepts in physics. The course includes: physics and measurements, vectors, motion in one and two dimensions, Newton's laws of motion and their applications, work and energy, rotational dynamics, rolling motion, conservation of angular momentum.

courses.title: General Physics II
courses.description: This course aims to provide students with a strong understanding of electricity and magnetism. In the electricity topics, the fundamental concepts of Coulomb's law, electric field, Gauss’s law, electric potential, capacitance and dielectrics, electric current, resistance, direct current circuits and Kirchhoff’s rules, and RC circuits are introduced. In the magnetism topics, magnetic field and magnetic forces, sources of magnetic fields, electromagnetic induction and Maxwell's Equations are introduced. Upon successful completion of the course, students will acquire good understanding of physics concepts and enhance their problem-solving abilities using basic vector calculus, techniques of summation and integration and solution of systems of equations. Students will be able to apply the concept of electricity and magnetism in solving problems related to everyday life examples.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D; MATH105 with a minimum grade D or MATH130 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
MATH105 with a minimum grade D or MATH130 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: General Physics Lab I
courses.description: The course aims at developing a clear understanding of the basic concepts in classical mechanics; Consolidating the manual skill in dealing with laboratory equipment; Developing skills of using computers in analysis of the computer interfaced experiments; It includes Fine measurements, free falling, motion on an inclined plane, verification of newton’s second law, Conservation of energy simple pendulum and circular motion.
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS105

courses.title: General Physics Lab II
courses.description: This course aims to develop a clear understanding of the basic concepts in electricity and magnetism; It includes: Coulomb's Law, equipotential surfaces and electric field lines, Ohm's Law, Kirchhoff's Rules, resistance and resistivity, potentiometer, capacitors, RC time constant, magnetic fields, oscilloscope, electromagnetic induction.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS135
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS110

courses.title: Introduction to Space Sciences
courses.description: This course will serve to give an overview of the domain of Space Sciences. It is intended to lay the foundations of what Space Sciences entail. It will start off with an outline of the characteristics of Earth as a planet and then it will take students immediately beyond Earth, the upper atmosphere and the magnetosphere of the Earth will be introduced. In addition to Earth as a planet, the formation of Solar System, planetary science: terrestrial & jovian planets, planetary atmosphere and interiors will also be discussed. Followed by that some basic features of space above the Earth and the concepts of gravity will be highlighted. Then, a brief history of human space exploration will be given, leading to an outline of the space age we live in today. The course will be concluded with a broad account of what science is done from space.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D; MATH105 or MATH130
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Intermediate Physics Lab I
courses.description: This course aims at developing a clear understanding of the basic concepts in waves, vibrations and optics. It includes: free damped oscillations, forced oscillations, interference of sound waves, standing waves, combination of two waves at right angles, combination of two waves with different frequency, spherical mirror and thin lenses, the optical spectrometer, interference of light waves, Mickelson interferometer, Newton’s rings, diffraction of light waves and polarization of light waves.
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS235

courses.title: Intermediate Physics Lab II
courses.description: This course aims at developing an understanding of the basic experiments in thermal and modern physics. It includes: thermometer, Stefan-Boltzmann's law, thermal radiation, photoelectric effect, electron diffraction, magnetic hysteresis, Faraday effect, Frank-Hertz experiment, Zeeman effect, Motion of charges in a uniform magnetic field, and x-ray diffraction
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS140
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS250; PHYS220

courses.title: Programming for Space Science
courses.description: This course is aimed at students with little to no programming experience. It will provide students an understanding about the computation and its role in solving space science related problems. It also aims to help students, feel confident in their ability to write simple programs that allow them to accomplish useful goals. The course will use Python as a programming language. The course will introduce the use of Linux as an operating system for Astronomy & Space Science. Also, commonly used python libraries as NumPy, SciPy and Astropy will be introduced.
courses.prerequisiteText: CSBP119 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: CSBP119 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Thermal Physics
courses.description: This course aims at developing an understanding of the main concepts, fundamental laws, and applications of classical thermodynamics. It includes definitions of the most important thermodynamic properties, including temperature, pressure, equation of state, internal energy, work, thermodynamic potentials, free energy functions and entropy, as well as, introducing the three fundamental laws of thermodynamics that govern every physical system in the universe. In addition, this course develops a working knowledge of some practical applications of thermodynamics in daily life, including air conditioners, refrigerators, and car engines.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Introduction to Astronomy & Space Sciences
courses.description: This foundational course introduces students to the vast domain of astronomy and space sciences, providing a comprehensive overview of the field's key concepts and methodologies.Topics include the study of our place in the Universe, distances, the solar system, our sun and stars. Students will explore fundamental astrophysical concepts such as gravity, light, and telescopic observation. The course also covers the history and evolution of human space exploration, from early observations to the modern space age.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Electronics Fundamentals
courses.description: The course covers the principles of semiconductor materials, followed by an in-depth analysis of semiconductor devices such as diodes, bipolar junction transistors, field-effect transistors, and operational amplifiers. Emphasis is placed on the structure, operation, biasing techniques, and practical applications of these devices.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Electronics Lab
courses.description: This course aims at developing clear understanding of the basic concepts of direct current circuits, fundamental laws of alternating current circuits, and the principles of semiconductor-based devices such as diodes and BJT transistors. Students conduct hands-on experiments on Direct current circuits, Alternating current circuits, diode characteristic curve, diode applications, special purpose diodes, Bipolar junction transistor (BJT) characteristic curve, BJT bias circuits, and BJT applications.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS233 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS233 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Waves and Optics
courses.description: This course aims at developing clear understanding of basic concepts in vibrations, waves, light and optics. It includes oscillatory motion, wave motion, sound waves, superposition and standing waves, electromagnetic waves, the nature of light, laws of geometric optics, image formation by lenses and mirrors, some optical instruments, interference, diffraction and polarization of light
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS205

courses.title: Modern Physics
courses.description: This course discusses the progress of modern physics. It introduces students to the foundations and principles of modern physics. The course will discuss some of the problems faced physicists at end of the nineteenth century. The course will provide a valuable theoretical introduction and an overview of the fundamental applications of the principles of modern physics in our world. Topics include the special theory of relativity, particle-like properties of light, wave-like properties of particles, early atom models, Basics of quantum mechanics, elementary particles, and Universe.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH105 with a minimum grade D; PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH105 with a minimum grade D
PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS210

courses.title: Mathematical Physics
courses.description: This course aims at developing the mathematical techniques and skills needed for advanced physics courses. The course covers the following topics: vector analysis, complex analysis, Fourier series and transforms with applications, series solutions to ODEs, and special functions.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH110 with a minimum grade D; PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH110 with a minimum grade D
PHYS105 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Modern Astrophysics
courses.description: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of stellar astrophysics, covering the formation, structure, evolution, and end states of stars. Students will learn the physical principles behind stellar interiors, atmospheres, nucleosynthesis, and explosive phenomena such as supernovae. The course also delves into variable stars, binary systems, and their role in distance measurement and cosmic evolution. A dedicated section on observational techniques introduces students to key methods such as spectroscopy, photometry, and interferometry, while computational modeling covers tools and simulations used to analyze stellar processes. Through both theoretical frameworks and real-world data analysis, students will gain a deep understanding of stellar evolution and its broader implications for galaxy formation and cosmic chemical enrichment. This course is designed to bridge classical astrophysics concepts with modern advancements, preparing students for further research and contributions in the field of astrophysics.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS225 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS225 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Classical Mechanics
courses.description: The course aims at studying the classical kinematics and dynamics of the point-like objects and the rigid bodies. It includes: particle kinematics in various coordinate systems, particle dynamics, central-force motion, non-inertial systems, rigid-body dynamics, introduction to Hamilton and Lagrange dynamics.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH275 with a minimum grade D or PHYS255 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH275 with a minimum grade D or PHYS255 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Celestial Mechanics
courses.description: This course will begin with the development of an understanding of Kepler’s laws of orbital motion and dynamics of objects in space. After that, the framework of celestial coordinate systems will be built followed by the 2-body/3-body problem. A description of the 6 orbital Parameters will be given after that. Then the fundamentals behind the Lagrange’s planetary equation will be presented, followed by an outline of the possible orbital perturbations. Some examples of natural & artificial orbits will be discussed and finally orbit and trajectory design for various space science objectives will be discussed.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH275 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH275 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Missions
courses.description: This course will be aimed at presenting an overview of a space mission as whole. The elements of a space mission will be introduced from a design and analysis point of view. Followed by that the space segment and the ground segment will be discussed as two main domains of a space mission, leading to an outline of space mission operations. The course will end with a few case studies (e.g. the GPS network, Telecom missions [ArabSat], science missions [MRO, Juno, Cassini]) of existing space missions.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS110

courses.title: Statistical Physics
courses.description: This course aims at developing a clear understanding of the basic concepts in statistical physics as an integrated part of the student's overall curriculum. It includes the kinetic theory of gases, equilibrium statistical distributions, including Maxwell-Boltzmann, Fermi-Dirac, Bose-Einstein, and their applications in the theories of the heat capacity of diatomic gases, the heat capacity of a solid, and the statistical thermodynamics of magnetism.
courses.preCorequisiteText: PHYS220 with a minimum grade D
preCorequisiteItems: PHYS220 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Spacecraft Instrument Science
courses.description: The contents of this course will develop an introduction to various subsystems of a spacecraft. The first topic will describe the components of a space vehicle followed by an account of the spacecraft materials used to build the structure. After that, some examples of the spacecraft’s main payload (spectrographs and spectrometers, imaging systems, space-based telescopes, radars and antennae) will be discussed. The functionality of the spacecraft attitude & orbit determination be highlighted next. After that, a brief account of the communication and navigation systems will be given. Then, the spacecraft power system will be described followed by an account of the spacecraft propulsion system. The fundamentals of spacecraft positioning control will be discussed in the end.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS235 with a minimum grade D; PHYS250 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS235 with a minimum grade D
PHYS250 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Sustainability
courses.description: This course addresses the critical challenges of sustaining the space environment amidst rapidly growing governmental and commercial activity. Students will explore orbital debris management, satellite end-of-life protocols, space situational awareness (SSA), and the ethical dimensions of space exploration. Topics include sustainable space mission design, in-situ resource utilization (ISRU), and space traffic management. International policies and agreements, such as the Outer Space Treaty and related UN guidelines, are examined alongside emerging national and commercial practices. Through case studies and a final project, students learn to evaluate risks, navigate legal and governance frameworks, and propose realistic solutions that support long-term, responsible use of outer space. The course incorporates hands-on learning through laboratory sessions, simulations, and design exercises, where students model orbital debris evolution, assess collision risks, evaluate ISRU trade-offs, and develop sustainability metrics for space missions.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Computational Physics
courses.description: This course aims at introducing the basic concepts and principles of numerical methods. It includes: principles of numerical analysis, some important numerical algorithms, mathematical modeling of physical systems, application of numerical techniques to mathematical models, computer simulation of physical systems, the Monte-Carlo method with some applications.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH140 with a minimum grade D; PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH140 with a minimum grade D
PHYS110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Communications & Navigation
courses.description: This course delves into the principles and technologies enabling communication and navigation in space. Topics include signal transmission, modulation, error correction, and data relay through satellites and deep-space networks. Students will explore navigation techniques, such as GPS, celestial navigation, and autonomous navigation for interplanetary missions. Real-world applications include satellite communication, Mars rover operations, and space-based services. Hands-on projects will involve analyzing signal data and designing basic communication protocols. This course equips students to understand and develop robust systems for efficient communication and navigation in space missions.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Electromagnetic Theory I
courses.description: The course aims at establishing the basic knowledge of the static electric and magnetic fields. It includes: electrostatics: Gauss law, electric fields in materials, polarization, boundary-value problems, Laplace and Poisson equations; magnetostatics: Biot-Savart’s law, Ampere’s law, scalar and vector potentials, magnetization of materials, Faraday’s law, and Maxwell's equations.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS255 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS255 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Laser Physics
courses.description: The course is intended to develop a clear understanding of the physical foundations of laser operation, laser systems and laser applications. Moreover, the course aims at developing the student's problem solving, skills and creative thought needed to meet modern high technology challenges. The course covers: The basic concepts of laser operation, properties of laser beams, spontaneous and stimulated emission, production of population inversion, optical resonator, pumping process, rate equations with transient & steady state solutions, laser types and applications in science and technology.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS250

courses.title: Quantum Mechanics I
courses.description: This course aims at developing a clear understanding of the fundamentals (concepts, postu-lates, and mathematical structure) of quantum mechanics. It aims also at developing the basic quantitative skills necessary in solving quantum mechanical problems.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D; MATH275 with a minimum grade D or PHYS255 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D
MATH275 with a minimum grade D or PHYS255 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Science Instrumentation
courses.description: This course delves into the design, principles, and operation of instruments used in space science research. Students will study key technologies such as cameras, spectrometers, telescopes, etc.. The course covers instrumentation challenges, including the spacecraft environment, spacecraft materials, and spacecraft attitude and orbit control. Also, the course covers spacecraft subsystems and technical instruments, such as for instance spacecraft command and data handling, propulsion, and power management. Students will explore real-world applications through case studies, such as for instance the Hubble Space Telescope and Mars rovers. Hands-on projects will familiarize students with the design and calibration of space science instruments. By integrating scientific knowledge and hands-on projects, the course will equip students to contribute to the development of next-generation space exploration tools.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS310 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space and Atmospheric Physics
courses.description: This course provides an understanding of fundamental concepts of physics governing Earth's neutral atmosphere and plasma in the space environment. Students will explore Earth’s middle/upper atmosphere, ionosphere, and magnetosphere. That includes physical properties and processes, such as composition, structure, and dynamics. Also, students will focus on solar-terrestrial interactions, including phenomena like space weather, geomagnetic storms, and aurora. Applications to spacecraft missions, spacecraft operations, and space/atmospheric science will be emphasized. This course lays the groundwork for understanding the complex interactions within Earth’s upper atmosphere and the space environment and their implications for robotic and human activities in space. By integrating scientific knowledge and computer experiments/observational data, this course prepares students to analyze data from spacecraft and ground-based instruments.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS335 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS335 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Radiation Physics
courses.description: This course aims at covering topics in radiation and its uses. It includes: types and sources of radiation, radioactive decay processes and energy release involved in decay schemes, interaction of radiation with matter, radiation tracks and stopping power.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Introduction to Astrophysics
courses.description: The wonders of the Universe and mysteries of the outer space fascinates every human being living on planet Earth. We all find ourselves inherently curious about the objects, events and the related phenomenon, and we strive to know more about it. Astrophysics, as a subject, provides us with the framework to apply laws and theories of Physics to behaviour of various objects and events in the Universe in order build an understanding of their nature, properties and origin. This course is all about how can we best utilize our knowledge of Physics to know more about our Universe in a systematic and scientific way.
courses.prerequisiteText: MATH110 with a minimum grade D; PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: MATH110 with a minimum grade D
PHYS105 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Planetary Science and Exoplanets
courses.description: This course explores the structure, formation, and evolution of planets within and beyond our Solar System. Students will study planetary surfaces, atmospheres, and interiors, focusing on the comparative analysis of terrestrial and Jovian planets. Also, they will study and compare small solar system bodies. The discovery and characterization of exoplanets, including techniques such as transit photometry and radial velocity, will be examined in detail. The course addresses critical questions about planet habitability and the search for life beyond Earth. Students will also analyze selected data/images from space missions (missions related to planetary science and/or exoplanets). By integrating scientific knowledge and observational data, this course equips students with the tools to study planetary systems comprehensively.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS225 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS225 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Applications I
courses.description: The Space Applications I course will serve the purpose of introducing the main areas of space science research. An account of remote sensing, earth observation & Geographic Information System will be given followed by the topics of study in space physics. Astronomy & Astrophysics will be outlined as the study of the processes and objects in the Universe. The course will be concluded with the concepts supporting data & image processing and some tools (introduction to Python, IDL and Matlab) and working knowledge of techniques (data analysis & interpretation) will also be developed as an essential skill set to carry out scientific research in the relevant areas of space science introduced in the course.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS200 with a minimum grade D; PHYS235 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS200 with a minimum grade D
PHYS235 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Galaxies and Cosmology
courses.description: This course provides an introduction to galaxies and cosmology, covering the structure and evolution of galaxies, the principles of cosmic expansion, and the role of dark matter. Students will explore active galactic nuclei, the Big Bang theory, and observational techniques like redshift surveys and gravitational lensing. The course also examines the large-scale structure of the universe and the cosmological models that describe its formation and growth.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS260 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS260 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Applications II
courses.description: This course will discuss presenting some more areas of research in space sciences. Firstly, the fundamentals of positioning guidance & navigation using space-based systems will be introduced. Followed by that, an outline of the themes related to atmospheric & ionospheric physics will be given. After that, modern communication achieved with space-based systems will be discussed. The last space applications theme to be outlined will be weather monitoring and prediction using spacecraft. The development of working knowledge of various tools and techniques will continue in this course as well, particularly relevant to the areas covered in this course.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS410 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS410 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Electromagnetic Theory II
courses.description: The course aims at using Maxwell's equations in treating specific problems of wave propagation and their interactions with media and charged particles. It includes wave equation propagation of electromagnetic waves in non-conducting media, polarization. Waves in bounded regions: reflection and refraction at dielectric interface, guided waves. Radiation from a group of moving charges, radiation damping. Electrodynamics and special relativity.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS335

courses.title: Quantum Mechanics II
courses.description: The course aims at developing the student’s fundamental knowledge in Quantum Mechanics. The course introduces several modern concepts in quantum mechanics that include propagators and path integral, symmetries, angular momentum and irreducible tensor operators, approximation methods, and scattering theory.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS355

courses.title: Solid State Physics
courses.description: Students in this course will learn about: crystalline structure and symmetry, Bravais lattice and reciprocal lattice, lattice vibrations and phonons, specific heat, energy band theory of metals, semiconductors and insulators, electric transport in metals and semiconductors, optical, dielectric, and magnetic properties, superconductivity.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS220 with a minimum grade D; PHYS250 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS220 with a minimum grade D
PHYS250 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Semiconductor Physics
courses.description: This course will provide students with a solid understanding of the physical principles of basic semiconductor devices. This course will give the students an overview of the development of semiconductor devices. Several important semiconductor physics and prototypical devices will be studied. The course material covers semiconductor properties under thermal equilibrium and under non-equilibrium conditions. Three fundamental device structures will be covered in detail, the p-n junction, the MOSFET and related devices, and the bipolar transistor. The course will focus on aspects of semiconductors such as silicon and gallium arsenide, both of which have commercial relevance. Therefore, fundamental properties of semiconductors will be explored, as well as their device applications.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS231

courses.title: Introductory Nuclear Physics
courses.description: This course covers basic concepts of nuclear physics with emphasis on Rutherford’s nuclear atom model, nuclear properties (nuclear size, mass and abundance of nuclides, nuclear binding energy), nuclear structures and nuclear models (Liquid-drop model and the semi-empirical mass formula, and the shell model). Other topics include nuclear decay and radioactivity, nuclear reactions (fundamental Laws, scattering and reaction cross section, mechanisms of nuclear reactions), nuclear fission (characteristics of fission, energy in fission, fission nuclear reactors), nuclear fusion (basic fusion processes, characteristics of fusion, controlled fusion reactors).
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS250 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Research Project
courses.description: This course aims at developing the students’ theoretical and/or experimental research skills necessary for conducting a scientific research project under the guidance of a faculty member. A real-life or active research problem is identified by the instructor and students. Students use their knowledge and get trained on methods to solve the problem. Students will be trained on, literature survey, team work, interpreting their results, implementing the ethics of scientific research, and communicating the whole investigation by means of a written report and an oral presentation.
courses.corequisiteText: PHYS500

courses.title: Selected Topics
courses.description: Physics is a field that is constantly expanding and evolving, with new discoveries and technologies emerging all the time. This course aims to cover selected topics dealing with the recent advances in the field of Physics and Astrophysics. The course will discuss the current knowledge of new emerging topics in modern Physics and related technology. Students will be required to read up on primary literature and make an oral presentation to the whole class on a chosen topic.

courses.title: Internship
courses.description: Students usually choose internship organizations that offer them an opportunity to apply in a supervised manner what they learned in their studies in a practical manner and to apply their rigorous coursework in a professional and industrial setting. In addition to its direct benefits to the student it consolidates the department bonds with the outside world and offers a real opportunity to get feedback about the teaching programs and educational services it offers.
courses.preCorequisiteText: PHYS494 with a minimum grade D
preCorequisiteItems: PHYS494 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Introduction to Renewable Energy Technology (PHYS501 )
courses.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to renewable energy systems, integrating fundamental physical principles with engineering applications and economic analysis. Beginning with the basic concepts of energy flow and resource characterization, students explore the major renewable technologies: solar photovoltaics, solar thermal systems, wind energy, hydropower, and bioenergy. The course then addresses cross-cutting themes including energy efficiency in the built environment and industrial processes, as well as energy economics. Through worked examples and a case study (e.g., solar farm with storage), students gain the quantitative skills to evaluate, compare, and design renewable energy systems in real-world contexts.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Fundamentals of Energy Storage Technologies (PHYS502 )
courses.description: This course introduces undergraduate science and engineering students to the fundamental principles, technologies, and applications of modern energy storage systems. The course focuses on the physical and operational principles of electrochemical and thermal energy storage. Students will gain an understanding of batteries, supercapacitors, thermal storage systems, and the key techniques used to characterize their performance.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Physics
courses.description: This course will serve to give an overview of the Physics of near-Earth space. It is intended to build the understanding of physical processes occurring immediately above planet Earth. It will start off with an outline of the characteristics and properties of space plasma including a discussion of various species of particles and their behavior. Followed by that, it will cover the topics related to Earth’s magnetosphere. Then, the aspects of Solar activity along with the elements of Solar-Terrestrial interaction will be highlighted. After that, an account of the characteristics of space weather and its effects on Earth will be given. The students will then be introduced to cosmic radiation, its origins and its interaction with Earth’s atmosphere. Moreover, the dynamics of near-Earth objects such as Asteroids, Meteors and Comets will be discussed including the tracking and mitigation of space debris. In addition, the environment and characteristics of unmagnetized objects (Mars, Venus) and magnetized objects (Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) will also be highlighted). Then, a brief history of human space exploration will be given, leading to an outline of the space age we live in today. The course will be concluded with an overview of the methods of space physics research.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D; PHYS110 with a minimum grade D; MATH105 with a minimum grade D; MATH110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
MATH105 with a minimum grade D
MATH110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Astronomy & Astrophysics
courses.description: This course will develop a good understanding of various astrophysical processes involved in the formation and evolution of astronomical objects such as stars, planets, galaxies. After a brief overwiew about the history of astronomy, we will discuss the fundamentals of celestial and Newtonian mechanics. We will also introduce various types of telescopes, their usability in astronomical observations and how to measure the distances within the solar system and between stars. Students will learn about about fundamental of photometry and spectroscopy. This will enable to them to interpret the stellar spectra and how to mearue brightness and fluxes. Formation of spectral lines in stellar atmospheres and Hertzsprun-Russell Diagram will be discussed in detail. This course will provide a detailed undesrtanding of star formation, stellar evolution and stellar interiors. This course will conclude by giving an overview of galaxy formation and their classification based on the Hubble sequence.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D; PHYS110 with a minimum grade D; MATH105 with a minimum grade D; MATH110 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS105 with a minimum grade D
PHYS110 with a minimum grade D
MATH105 with a minimum grade D
MATH110 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Methods of Mathematical Physics
courses.description: Complex analysis, special functions with applications in Physics, calculus of variations, integral transforms, partial differential equations, boundary-value problems, Green’s functions, operator algebra and tensors.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS255

courses.title: Quantum Physics I
courses.description: The course presents the basic concepts and mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics and introduces applications in atomic, molecular, and solid-state Physics. Topics include the mathematics of quantum mechanics, one-dimensional problems, central field problems, the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with atomic systems, the harmonic oscillator, angular momentum, and perturbation theory.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS355 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS355 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Electrodynamics I
courses.description: Electrostatics and magnetostatics, Electric and magnetic fields in matter, Boundary value problems in electrostatics and magnetostatics, Polarization and magnetization, Multipole expansion and dielectrics, Maxwell’s equations, Conservation laws, Wave guides and resonators.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS335

courses.title: Atomic Physics
courses.description: Electronic structure of one-electron atoms; fine and hyperfine structures, Interaction of one-electron atoms with static external electric and magnetic fields and with electromagnetic radiation. Study of the electronic structure of many-electron atoms using Pauli Exclusion principle, perturbation and variational methods, angular momentum coupling schemes, central field approximation, Thomas-Fermi model, Hartee-Fock method, interactions of many-electron atoms with static and magnetic fields and electromagnetic radiation, Auger effect. Study the structure of molecules and their rotational, vibrational, and electronic structure
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS250

courses.title: Advanced Laser Physics
courses.description: The course is intended to introduce the fundamental concepts of laser theory and the interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter. The course covers: the concepts of laser operation, absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission, optical resonator, pumping sources, laser oscillation (gain and threshold), the modulation of optical radiation, Q- switching and mode locking. Moreover, the course aims at developing the student's problem solving, skills and creative thought needed to meet modern high technology challenges.

courses.title: Analytical Mechanics
courses.description: Elementary principles, variational principles and Lagrange's equations, central force problem, kinematics of rigid body motion, oscillations, Hamilton's principle and Hamilton's equations, Canonical transformations, Hamilton-Jacobi theory, classical chaos, canonical perturbation theory, introduction to Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations for continuous systems and fields.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS262 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS262 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Nuclear Physics
courses.description: Nuclear Properties (Nuclear Radius, Mass and Abundance of Nuclides, Nuclear Binding Energy), Forces between Nucleons (Properties of the Nuclear Force, The Exchange Force Model), Nuclear Structures and Nuclear Models (Liquid-drop Model and the Semi-empirical Mass Formula, Shell Model, More Realistic Nuclear Models), Nuclear Decay and Radioactivity, Nuclear Reactions (Fundamental Laws, Scattering and Reaction Cross Section, The Optical Model, Mechanisms of Nuclear Reactions), Neutron Physics (Neutron Sources, Absorption and Moderation, Neutron Reaction Cross Sections, Neutron Capture, Interference and Diffraction with Neutrons), Nuclear Fission (Characteristics of Fission, Energy in Fission, Fission Reactors, Radioactive Fission Products, Fission Explosives), Nuclear Fusion (Basic Fusion Processes, Characteristics of Fusion, Controlled Fusion Reactors, Thermonuclear Weapons).
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS355

courses.title: Introduction to Plasma Physics
courses.description: This course covers elementary plasma physics for physics and engineering students. It includes an introduction to the plasma state and occurrence, motion of single charged particles in static and time varying electric and magnetic fields, plasmas described as (charged) fluids or magnetohydrodynamics; waves in plasmas, kinetic theory description of plasmas, Vlasov equation and collisionless plasmas, collisions and transport properties, in addition to a discussion of nuclear fusion.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS335 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS335 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Elementary Particle Physics
courses.description: Description of elementary particles with emphasis on phenomenology and historical and experimental buildup of current knowledge: weak decays and weak currents, parity violation, detectors and accelerators, elementary processes, deep inelastic scattering and proton model, quark model spectroscopy, color symmetry, elements of the Standard Model, successes and shortcomings.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS525

courses.title: Physics of Semiconductors
courses.description: This course gives students a solid background in semiconductor Physics and devices. It explains crystal structure, band structure and carrier statistics, carrier transport, phonons, scattering processes, electro- and optical- absorption in semiconductors.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS470 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS470 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Space Science Instrumentation
courses.description: This course aims at presenting an account of various instruments and facilities used in space science. It will start off with a description and classification of the types of space science instruments such as spectrometers, spectrographs, telescopes, cameras, sensors, imagers and detectors. Followed by that, the scientific principles behind these instruments and the physics of detector operation will be discussed. Then, an understanding of the inputs and outputs of these instruments will be developed. The interpretation of the variations in the observable signatures of physical phenomena will also be discussed. After that, the students will be given an overview of the platforms and facilities on which the space science instruments operate. This topic will include case studies of space missions. A brief outline of some of the specifications and technical characteristics will also be covered.

courses.title: Modern Statistical Physics
courses.description: Review of the statistical theory of thermodynamics, Ensemble theory, identical particles. Quantum statistical Physics, Distribution functions, Applications to Quantum gases (superfluidity, superconductivity, and Bose-Einstein condensation), Critical phenomena, Brownian motion, Langevin, and Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann equations.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS312

courses.title: Solid-State Physics I
courses.description: Students in this course will learn about: crystalline structure and symmetry, Bravais lattice and reciprocal lattice, lattice vibrations and phonons, specific heat, energy band theory of metals, semiconductors and insulators, electric transport in metals and semiconductors, optical, dielectric, and magnetic properties, superconductivity.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS355 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS355 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Computational Physics-I
courses.description: Classical and quantum Monte Carlo simulation methods with applications, molecular dynamics simulations, random systems, selected topics in modern computational physics problems.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS330 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS330 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Physics Seminar
courses.description: This course is based on a research project where the student is expected to present a seminar at the end of the semester. The topic is selected by the faculty member. Ethics issues related to physics research will be also discussed.

courses.title: Space Science Internship
courses.description: The primary objective of this internship course is to afford the MSc Space Science students a supervised opportunity to acquire practical and hands-on working experience at one of the reputed space research and development organizations in the UAE. Within the scope of this internship, the students will be attached to teams of researchers, engineers and scientists at the internship provider site (e.g. UAE Space Agency, Muhammad Bin Rashid Space Centre) to work on practical tasks which will be components of actual and ongoing space projects. Availing this opportunity, students will be able to apply the knowledge they attained as part of their MSc coursework, get first-hand experience in a professional space research setting, learn practical aspects of problem solving, solution development, teamwork, project execution and delivery, and it will also benefit them in terms of skill development and capacity building.

courses.title: Internship
courses.description: This course provides Master of Science in Physics students with structured, supervised work experience in a professional setting that is directly related to the application of physics. Students will engage in practical scientific or technical tasks within research laboratories, industry, education, or other approved organizations. The internship is designed to bridge academic study with real-world practice, allowing students to apply core physics knowledge, analytical skills, and problem solving in authentic work environments. Students will document their internship activities and outcomes in a written report that clearly describes their work, results, and learning.

courses.title: Capstone Project
courses.description: This course serves as the culminating academic experience for students enrolled in the non-thesis Master’s program in Physics. It offers an opportunity to engage in meaningful research through the completion of an independent capstone project conducted under faculty supervision. The capstone is designed to integrate and synthesize knowledge gained from prior coursework, foster critical analysis of scientific literature, and strengthen professional-level written and oral communication skills. While the project involves rigorous analysis and disciplined inquiry, it does not require original or publishable research and is distinct in scope and expectations from a traditional Master’s thesis. Within a structured academic framework, the course demonstrates students’ ability to apply advanced physics concepts to a clearly defined problem. The capstone extends across two consecutive semesters to allow for sustained investigation and comprehensive reporting of results.

courses.title: Selected Topics I
courses.description: This course will develop a good understanding of various astrophysical processes involved in the star formation. After a brief overview about the interstellar medium and molecular cloud , we will discuss the atomic and molecular gas observations using radio observations and students will be given worked-out examples. We will also introduce detailed observational properties of molecular clouds, physics of molecular cloud, structure and kinematics and various scaling relation, and initial mass function to understand the star processes. High-mass star feedback processes will be introduced with the HII region physical processes. The cloud properties such as column densities, virial-mass, and LTE mass will be discussed. This course will also introduce various astronomical tools and codes for studying the molecular cloud and HII region properties using radio and optical observational data.

courses.title: Quantum Physics II
courses.description: Variational theorem and WKB method, time-dependent perturbation theory, scattering theory, Born approximation, Identical particles and second quantization, symmetry principles, Dirac and Klein-Gordon equations for free particles, quantum theory of radiation, path integral formalism.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS525

courses.title: Synthesis, Characteristics & Applications of Nanomaterials
courses.description: Synthesis of nanomaterials; nanoparticles, nanotubes, nanowires, assembly of nanostructures, property-structure-dependence in nanomaterials, main characterization techniques; transmission electron microscopy (TEM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), applications of nanomaterials; transistors, bio-sensors, NEMS, and solar cells.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS470 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS470 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Quantum Field Theory
courses.description: Building the theory of relativistic quantum fields: classical field theory; Noethers's theorem; Klein Gordon field; representations of the Lorentz Group; Dirac equation; quantized Dirac field; discrete symmetries of the Dirac theory; interacting fields; S-matrix and reduction formula; Green’s functions in path integral formalism; perturbation theory and Feynman diagrams; elementary processes in QED and QCD.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS530 with a minimum grade D; PHYS525 with a minimum grade D
prerequisiteItems: PHYS530 with a minimum grade D
PHYS525 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Solid State Physics II
courses.description: This is a one-semester advanced course intended for physics graduate students. It will cover the foundational principles of solid state physics, with an emphasis on the application of quantum theory to the atomic and electronic structure of crystalline solids.This course will follow the approach taken in texts such as Ashcroft and Mermin, I will also use materials from Joseph Callaway. The first part deals with the Drude and Sommerfeld models of electrical conduction, the failures of both models, we will make extensive use of your knowledge of statistical physics and quantum mechanics. The second part of the course teaches the electronic band theory from the basics which describes the electronic states of solids. The "nearly free-electron model" and the "tight-binding approximation" will be introduced. First-principles electron theory is discussed as one of the most important topics in advanced solid state physics. Then, density functional theory is introduced. Applications to the electronic states of low-dimensional materials and metallic microstructure interfaces are discussed to deepen the understanding.

courses.title: Computational Physics-II
courses.description: The course aims at developing essential numerical analysis techniques such as classical and quantum Monte Carlo simulation methods with applications, molecular dynamics simulations, random systems, selected topics in modern computational physics problems.

courses.title: Electrodynamics II
courses.description: Review of Maxwell’s equations and the conservation laws, electromagnetic potentials, multipole radiation, radiation from moving charges, plane waves in material media, polarization, attenuation, dispersion, diffraction, scattering, special relativity, Relativistic electrodynamics.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS530

courses.title: Standard Model of Particle Physics
courses.description: This course covers: Theoretical building of the Standard Model of Particle Physics: phenomenology of weak interactions; Higgs mechanics and mass generation; spontaneously broken gauge theory; renormalization; the Standard Model; successes and shortcomings.

prerequisiteItems: PHYS525 with a minimum grade D

courses.title: Advanced Topics in Particle Theory
courses.description: This course covers selected and changing topics beyond and besides the Standard Model like: neutrinos and masses; solitons, instantons and topological objects; nonperturbative methods: lattice field theory; quantum field theory at finite temperature and/or density; LHC particle physics; string theory.
courses.prerequisiteText: PHYS782

courses.title: Selected Topics II
courses.description: Physics is a field that is constantly expanding and evolving, with new discoveries and technologies emerging all the time. This course aims to cover selected topics dealing with the recent advances in the field of Physics and Astrophysics. The course will discuss the current knowledge of new emerging topics in modern Physics and related technology. This course is proposed by faculty members based on students’ curricular needs and/or new trends in Physics.
